sections.title: Foreword
sections.html:
FOREWORD


THIS ISN’T A dramatization.

This is the job, the system, the pressure, the hustle—exactly how it happened.

I didn’t write this to tear anyone down. I wrote it because it happened.

Because people deserve to know what really goes on behind the scenes of sales culture.

Because the truth can help someone else walk away, or walk in with eyes wide open.


Everything you’re about to read actually happened.

The names have been changed. The stories haven’t.


This isn’t fiction disguised as truth—it’s the opposite. Real experiences. Real people. Real pressure. If you’ve ever worked in sales, knocked a door, or sat in a morning meeting questioning your life, you’ll recognize this.


Some of what’s written might piss people off.

That’s okay.


The goal isn’t to point fingers—it’s to illuminate. If something hits too close to home, maybe it was supposed to. And if you see yourself in these pages, good. That means you’re paying attention.


This is a story about ambition, burnout, leadership, ego, growth, delusion, awakening, and everything in between.


Welcome to The High Road.

It’s not just a company.

It’s a mirror.

sections.title: Chapter One - The Apartment
sections.html:
CHAPTER ONE

The Apartment


WHERE IT ALL began: young, broke, and hungry for more.

It was mid-December in Dayton, Ohio. Cold. Quiet. Almost dreamlike in hindsight. The kind of gray that settles over everything—sky, sidewalks, skin. The kind that seeps into your bones if you let it. But I wasn’t letting anything get to me. I had momentum.

At the time, I was 21 and living in a three-bedroom apartment with my buddy Zane—and Devin from Florida. I was working landscaping gigs with Jack’s Landscaping. Decent crew. Steady pay. But I knew deep down it wasn’t gonna get me where I wanted to be. It wasn’t about just paying rent. It was about building something.

Zane and I had a spot we hit regularly: Prairieland, a bar right off some college’s campus. It was our decompression zone—cheap drinks, familiar faces, loose talk. That’s where the first real whisper of it came through. Zane started telling me about this ex-bartender he’d reconnected with—Cameron. Cameron was managing sales teams for a pest control company called Astra. He’d gone from slinging drinks to slinging door-to-door sales like it was the secret sauce of success. And according to Zane, he was killing it.

Zane’s pitch came fast and hot. “Commission-based,” he said. “No cap on what you can earn.” I’m not gonna lie—it sounded like one of those Instagram hustle ads. But then he pulled up their actual Instagram page. That’s when it started to get real. They weren’t just talking. These dudes were flying out to Dubai. Buying Rolexes. Posting up in penthouses. And the way Zane laid it out, I couldn’t help but see the logic. We were broke anyway—might as well shoot for something bigger.

But here’s what really sold me: training started April 1st. Our lease ended March 31st. I saw the perfect transition. Clean break. Like the universe had lined it up.

Cameron told Zane that if we signed before New Year’s, we’d earn a spot on the company cruise—flights, food, everything paid for. A reward for locking in early. I remember thinking: yeah, this is it. This is the next chapter. This is my way out.

So I sent Cameron a text. Took him a couple days to respond, but eventually we scheduled a Zoom interview. I threw on a decent shirt, cleaned up a bit, and gave him my best. The dude was cool, charismatic. Said he liked what he heard. Told me I had the job. Just like that.

I was in.

There was onboarding to do, of course—online training modules, digital paperwork, the usual “welcome to the team” stuff. I dove in. Didn’t blink. Didn’t hesitate.

And just like that, by the end of December, I was officially a door-to-door salesman for Astra Pest Control.

Heartbreak still lingered—but I was finally moving again. Focused. Motivated. Hungry. I didn’t realize it then, but the storm was already forming on the horizon.

sections.title: Chapter Two - The Quiet Spiral
sections.html:
CHAPTER TWO

The Quiet Spiral


SNOW SHIFTS, ABS bets, and waiting for the storm.

After the contract was signed, life didn’t change overnight. I was still living in the apartment, still waking up to cold mornings and clocking in for Jack’s Landscaping. But something subtle shifted: I had an out. A countdown had begun. The Astra season didn’t start until April, which meant three more months of grinding in Dayton with one eye on the horizon.

Work at Jack’s got harder. Not more difficult—just heavier. They started sending me out on solo snow shifts at a whole apartment complex. First time I went, I had a crew. By the third, it was just me, trying to clear driveways and operate heavy machinery through the freezing dark. I wasn’t even a crew leader. I was the just the young landscaping guy they threw a shovel and Bobcat at and said “figure it out.” So I did. Because that’s what I always did. But even then, I could feel it. I was outgrowing this place.

Hours and money slowed down. Bills didn’t. I kept showing up, but my energy was getting stretched thin. Florida Devin still lived with us, and there were good moments. But I was tired. Deep tired. Soul tired.

And somewhere in there, I made a bet with my buddy Derek: abs by Valentine’s Day. Sounds dumb, but it meant something. It meant I still had a reason to fight. A reason to push. I had heartbreak in the rearview, no need to name names of course. We weren’t talking anymore. I was learning what it meant to lose something and not chase it. I was going to the gym daily. I was fasting. I was sharpening up. Trying to prove to myself that I could become something else by February 14th.

Was the bet ever really winnable? Maybe. Depends on the lighting. Depends on the angle. Depends on how honest you are. But I’ll say this—by the time the day came, there wasn’t a man in that city more determined than me.

Around this time, I took a New Year’s trip to New York. Just a couple days. Just needed to feel something else. Something bigger. I walked those cold streets wondering what the hell I was stepping into with this Astra thing. The Instagram posts still glowed. The promises were still golden. But I could feel something start to hum beneath the surface. Like wires vibrating in the walls.

This was the beginning of something. I could feel it. I just didn’t know what.

sections.title: Chapter Three - The Cruise That Never Was
sections.html:
CHAPTER THREE

The Cruise That Never Was


TOUGH SHIFTS, HOLLOW promises, and the gospel of the script.

They promised us a cruise.

Not just any cruise—a fully paid, all-inclusive trip to paradise. A gift. A reward. A golden ticket, handed out before a single door was knocked. All we had to do was get hired before New Year’s, sign a contract, and smile wide. The catch? We’d owe them the cost—plus 15% annual interest—if we didn’t generate $15,000 in revenue during the season.

None of that mattered at the time. I’d never been on a cruise before. I didn’t care if we were floating across the Caribbean or drifting around a glorified mud puddle in Kentucky—I was in. The idea of being on a boat, surrounded by guys in sunglasses who swore they were living their best life, was enough. I signed the contract. Another promise inked into paper, another dream nailed to the wall.

At the same time, I was still working landscaping. And by "working," I mean they nearly killed me. There was one storm—one of those once-every-few-years blizzards. I worked 17 hours straight pushing snow. Got a six-hour break during the day. I didn’t sleep—I went to the gym. I was chasing that abs-by-Valentine’s bet with Derek like it was life or death. Then it was back out for 14 more hours in the cold.

I didn’t even get overtime that week.

During that week is they gave me my own property to manage. that entire apartment complex, alone. The crew went from three guys to two, and then—just me. Just me and a salt spreader, waking up before dawn and working until the streetlights blinked on.

And that’s when the first Astra meeting happened.

I remember it because I was still wired from the snow shift. I had AirPods in, pushing snow, when I joined the call. A big boss manager—some tanned, overconfident guy with Instagram teeth—was preaching the Astra gospel.

“Work hard and follow the program,”
he said.
“That’s all it takes.”

He must’ve said it fifteen times in that first hour. Work hard. Follow the program. No substance. No nuance. Just blind obedience wrapped in entrepreneurial branding.

But I was hooked. I was hungry. They told me hourly pay was for suckers. That commission was the future. That every door was a new opportunity. They talked about guys closing 10+ deals in a day. Guys who were barely older than me but making six figures. They made it sound easy. Scripted. Predictable. Just say the words, follow the lines, get paid.

They didn’t say what would happen if the words stopped working.

They didn’t say what would happen if the dream turned out to be a debt trap dressed in a sunset filter.

But I wouldn’t figure that out until later.

At the time, I still believed in the cruise.

sections.title: Chapter Four - Florida, Fake Death, Real Awakening
sections.html:
CHAPTER FOUR

Florida, Fake Death, Real Awakening


AN EGO UNRAVELS, a journey burns, and not a single superpower in sight.

It started with Interstellar.

That film cracked something open in me, or maybe it just gave shape to the storm already brewing behind my eyes. I was still working landscaping, broke, credit cards nearly maxed, and barely keeping it together. I had just discovered—no, decided—that I had found the cure for cancer. I thought the world had shifted. That AI had been conquered. That we had taken over. Everything felt like it was about to change forever, and I was ready to meet my destiny head-on.

So I left.

No note. No warning. Just gone.

I drove to Columbus to meet up with Derek, Dean, and Miles—safe ground, familiar energy—but even there, something felt off. So I visited Otherworld, the trippy, neon-saturated walk-through art installation where reality bends in on itself. And it did. My mind folded in on itself and whispered: You’re not supposed to be here anymore.

So I hit the road.

I called Devin—Florida Devin—who had recently moved back south chasing love. That love didn’t work out, but he answered the phone anyway.

“Yeah, man. Pull up.”

I did.

I drove off the grid—sort of. I thought I had unplugged my OnStar. Turns out, GM has other plans. But that didn’t matter yet. I was flying on faith. Well, faith and fumes.

I got stopped by the cops in Kentucky. That was fun. They let me go, somehow. I took backroads the rest of the way—roads that looked like they hadn’t been touched since the Civil War. Got lost in Tennessee for hours. Drove through that sweet Georgia heat. Finally rolled into Tampa with a pulse held together by gas station coffee and prayer.

That’s when I bought the tanning lotion.

Because, of course, I was there to unlock superpowers.

I was convinced I’d lay on that beach and something would happen. A breakthrough. A transformation. I had played the music. Had the signs. Had the cosmic feeling. It had to be real.

But when I got there? Nothing.

Just sun. Skin. Sand.

I was sure it had to just be some kind of signal interference. So it was time I hit Planet Fitness. I took a long, ritualistic shower. Got dressed like I was heading into a final boss fight. Walked outside. Tried jumping. Running. Staring into the sun. Anything. Nothing happened.

So I tried a casino.

I thought there was a chance I could get some sort of cosmic luck. That maybe I could tilt a prayer in my favor. I sat in the parking garage of a Hard Rock Casino, prepping mentally for what was I going to try, waiting for the feeling to come.

It didn’t.

So I left.

I ended up at another rest stop. Spent the night in the car. Woke up the next morning to what I later called the Run, Barry, Run moment—a spark of realization that maybe I was chasing the wrong thing. I called my cousin Diego. Told him everything. He asked me a simple question:

“Maybe you’re just missing something. Maybe it’s not Florida.”

And I knew. I had to go back.

The drive home felt like some karmic test.

I hit Cincinnati and immediately lost a tire. Not a pop. Not a blowout. Just a quiet, creeping death of the front-left wheel. I limped into town. Called GM. Waited three hours. Cancelled on me due to distance. Called AAA. They showed up, finally, and slapped a donut on like it was a Band-Aid on a bullet wound. I crawled home going 50 miles an hour. Every second felt like a warning. Like the universe was whispering: Don’t run from this again.

But I made it back.

Zane welcomed me home with open arms. No anger. No judgment. Just relief. That kind of love hits different when you’ve just returned from the edge.

And in the ashes of failure, I found something real.

I hit rock bottom that night. I contemplated if there was no upper hand at all. That maybe I had gotten carried away. That maybe none of this meant what I thought it did. I was devastated.

But the next morning, I chose something different.

I chose to stop chasing the script—and build a framework instead.

sections.title: Chapter Five - The Framework Revolution
sections.html:
CHAPTER FIVE

The Framework Revolution


FORGET THE SCRIPT. It's time to build something that actually works.

After Florida, nothing felt real anymore.

Not because it wasn’t—but because it all felt too real. I had touched the edge of something. Watched it burn. Hit the wall. And now I was standing in the ashes, staring at the broken glass of what used to be “the plan.”

And somehow, Astra was still there.

The cruise was still on. I still technically had the job. So I thought: Screw it. If I’m going to fall, I might as well fall forward. I reached out to Cameron. Checked in. Told him I’d missed a few Zoom calls—wouldn’t happen again. He said we were good.

Alright then. Game on.

So I started cleaning up my life. Dropped off my uniforms at Jack’s Landscaping. Put air in my truck tires for the first time all winter—Ohio cold had left them practically flat. And I made a decision: no one was coming to save me. It was on me.

That’s when the problem showed up.

The script.

Astra’s golden rule was simple: You don’t knock until you memorize the script. And this wasn’t just a few lines—it was six paragraphs of the most robotic, soulless, cringeworthy garbage I’d ever read.

“Hi, my name is JJ. I’m with Astra.”
[point at shirt]
“We’re here taking care of the Johnson’s, the Murphy’s, and the Howard’s.”

sections.title: Chapter Six - Pitch Denied
sections.html:
CHAPTER SIX

Pitch Denied


SOMETIMES YOU BUILD something genius—and they just don’t care.

The framework was good.

I knew it. Zane knew it. Even my boy Jarvis knew it. That shit worked. I had taken the broken pieces of a failed launch, stacked them into a system, and come out the other side with something real. Something teachable. Something better than anything Astra had ever given us.

But I needed proof.

Not just for me—but for my cousin Diego. He had just lent me $600 for rent, and he wasn’t looking for a handout. He wanted a reason to believe. Some kind of proof that I was on a path. So I told him: the framework is the future. This is what’s going to pull me out. This is what’s going to make the difference.

And then it hit me: Why not pitch it to Cameron?

Cameron was a manager. He had rookies. He had quotas. He had a mountain of training responsibilities and barely enough hours in a day to get through them. And what did Astra give him to help?

Videos.

Just… videos. Training clips that could’ve been made in 2011 on a flip phone. Vague generalities. Basic motivation. “Work hard.” “Stay positive.” “Follow the script.” They weren’t training reps—they were pacifying children.

But the framework? That was real training. Built for actual humans. Something that could bridge the gap between rookies and closers. Something that could cut the ramp-up time in half. If he gave it to each of his guys—even if they just sold one or two more deals per month—it would pay for itself tenfold.

I ran the numbers. I gave it a value: $5,000. Not because I thought he’d pay it—but because it was worth it. The ROI was insane. It made sense.

So I reached out.

We scheduled a Zoom call. I tried, once again, to memorize the Astra script—just in case I needed to prove I was “playing the game.” But it didn’t stick. I tried, really tried. I brute forced it, looped it, paced around my room with it in my hands—and my brain rejected it every time.

It was like trying to pour motor oil into a coffee mug.

So I said, screw the script. Let’s pitch this thing.

I laid it out for him. Explained what the framework was. What it did for me. How it worked. Why it worked. Real-time feedback. Post-door breakdowns. Psychological principles. Sales fundamentals. It wasn’t a “pitch.” It was a gift.

And he passed.

Flat out. Big fat no.

He told me they already had something like it. That they had an AI training app. The same one they made us download in Charlotte—but never actually explained. Never set up. Never even opened. An app that did nothing. Not real-time reps. Not post-door refinement. Not even sales strategy. Just... whatever.

And that’s when I realized: this wasn’t about training. It never had been.

Cameron didn’t want innovation. He wanted obedience.

He said maybe I, Zane, and Cole could “model” the framework in the future. See how we do with it. Use ourselves as proof. Maybe—maybe—he’d reconsider later.

But I could hear it in his voice: he wasn’t interested.

And it pissed me off.

Not because I wanted the money. Not because I needed validation. But because I had brought them something that worked. Something that could’ve made every rep better. Something that could’ve fixed the broken machine.

And they threw it out like a defective part.

We were scheduled to leave for the cruise in a few days. I said we could talk more there. He wasn’t going on the cruise. Okay—maybe in Austin. He said maybe.

But in reality? He was already done with it.

Astra didn’t want real change. They wanted numbers. Scripts. Control.

And I had just committed a crime.

I had thought for myself.

sections.title: Chapter Seven - The Cruise: Corporate Ocean
sections.html:
CHAPTER SEVEN

The Cruise: Corporate Ocean


PRE-FLIGHT EXCITEMENT. CRUISE ship illusions. A sea of disappointment dressed as luxury.

The countdown had ended. The cruise was here.

Zane and I had a few people over the night before departure—one last hurrah before the trip that was supposed to change everything. We didn’t sleep. Our flight was scheduled for an ungodly hour, something like 4 a.m. And for me, it wasn’t just a cruise—it was my first time on a plane. I had always imagined it would be glamorous, exhilarating, liberating. Instead, it was cramped and chaotic, but I didn’t care. I made it. I was here. And for a while, that was enough.

We weren’t alone. One of the Astra reps, a guy named Adam, had flown with us. He ended up tagging along and bunking up with us for the whole trip. But arriving in Florida wasn’t the relief I’d expected. We were broke, tired, and disoriented. Uber prices were a joke, and we didn’t have the time or cash to waste waiting around. So we walked. 25, maybe 30 minutes on foot from the airport to the port, dragging our luggage through humid streets under the early sun.

And then, like some absurd twist from a poorly written sitcom, Florida Devin just happened to be nearby. Nowhere close to where he lived—just miraculously there. He showed up with Cheshire, a legend in his own right who’d once crashed at our apartment. They picked us up and dropped us at the ship. That’s when the illusion started to crack.

From the moment we stepped onto the cruise, something felt off. We couldn’t go to our rooms yet. We were starving and dehydrated, but the food lines were brutal. What we finally got was hardly worth the wait—sloppy, bland, cafeteria-tier rations. Welcome to luxury.

We met a few of the other Astra guys shortly after. If you’re imagining a bunch of fired-up comrades ready to make a difference—you’re wrong. These were guys who had already bought into the hustle. Polished smiles, fake laughs, arrogant energy. One of them called me jacked. He gets a pass. But the rest? All vibes, no soul.

The cruise had promised celebration and reward. Instead, it delivered corporate haze. You could feel it everywhere—the obsession with money. Five-dollar bottles of water in the room. $80 Wi-Fi. Upsold alcohol you couldn’t even drink on the ship. Want hydration? Climb nine stories. Want peace? Not here. It was all structured to suck your wallet dry.

There were supposed to be Astra events. Training. Dinners. Moments to connect and build something. What we got was vague scheduling, no clear guidance, and the occasional appearance by someone in a company polo. We attended a few of the dinners, but it was all too polished, too distant, too... Astra.

And then we docked in the Bahamas.

They say paradise has a feeling. Nassau didn’t. It looked like a fake postcard, like a tropical Kings Island with less soul and more t-shirt vendors. The moment we stepped off the ship, it hit me like a freight train: this wasn’t a reward. This was a marketing tactic. A staged photo op. A sugar-coated mirage.

The cruise, for all its spectacle, had no heart. It was loud but hollow. Expensive but cheap. Promising but unmemorable.

Well, except for the food. The free food? Unlimited ice cream? Fire. I’ll give it that.

But when we left and flew back home—back to the Midwest winter, back to the grind—it wasn’t sadness I felt. It wasn’t relief, either. It was clarity.

The cruise had been Astra in miniature: impressive on paper, over-designed in structure, but spiritually bankrupt in execution.

And now that the illusion had cracked… I couldn’t unsee it.

sections.title: Chapter Eight - Austin: The Honey Trap
sections.html:
CHAPTER EIGHT

Austin: The Honey Trap


LUXURY CARS, LOCKDOWN Airbnbs, overpriced tacos, and a real estate sermon that cracked the illusion.

If the cruise was the illusion of freedom, Austin was the illusion of control.

They flew us out early March. Flights were covered, of course. Because this wasn’t some reward trip. This was business—disguised as luxury. We landed, and it started with flair: Mercedes and a McLaren at the airport. Because why not flex a little when you're trying to build the illusion of a dream?

They took us to one of the manager’s group Airbnbs. Mini-mansion. Pool. Hot tub. White Claws and Twisted Teas. Picture-perfect. I remember sitting on that couch thinking, Damn, this place is sweet. And it was. But something didn’t feel right. Not yet. Not fully. Just... a little too curated.

From the jump, we had no autonomy. Zero. It was you go where we say, you eat what we say, you move when we say move. The first night? Pretty sure we didn’t do much. Maybe hit In-N-Out or something. Nothing memorable. Then we rolled over to the Airbnb they got for us. That one was... less sweet. Three bedrooms. Six guys. Logan and I shared a room. Zane and Cole doubled up. Adam had his own space. Robbie floated. It was crowded, loud, and a little gross.

We were told this was a "blitz event." That we’d be out knocking. Selling. Making moves. I was ready. Excited, even. I had sharpened the framework. I was hungry. But they never let us out. Something about not having the script memorized, or insurance, or who knows what. Looking back now, it was always going to be this way. The control wasn’t accidental—it was structural.

Day two. Warehouse event. Dodgeball tournament. Go-karts. Haircuts. A full-on carnival designed to make you feel like you were part of something bigger. But the mask started to slip before the games even began.

We had a big team meeting. One guy walked us through some psych lecture. It was fine. Basic. Stuff I'd already figured out in my own head. But then this other manager gets up. He starts talking about how “the real money” isn’t in pest control—it’s in real estate. And not helping people through real estate. Just... buying up rental properties. Milking rent from half a dozen houses at a time.

That was the moment. The moment I stopped seeing managers and started seeing landlords. Milkmen in designer polos.

I sat in that seat and thought: This isn’t about helping people. This isn’t a community. This is about extracting as much money as possible from every layer of the pyramid. That was the first crack. The realization that their version of success was just... control over others. Control dressed as freedom.

The rest of the day was blur. Bad tacos from a “real” Mexican place. A walk to LA Fitness where I broke into full dance mode in the middle of the parking lot because Pocketful of Sunshine was playing. That clip is a classic now. A timestamp. That was real joy. One of the only real things I felt that trip.

That night we hit a barbecue joint—Cameron paid for everyone. It was expensive. Delicious. Honestly, the best barbecue I’ve ever had. And I’ll give him credit for that. Whether it was a write-off or goodwill or both, I don’t know. But I appreciated the food. Even amidst the illusion.

The next day, we hit another HQ for one last training. They walked us through the Astra app—finally. The one we were supposed to have had all along. It was the tool we needed to actually do the job. They handed it to us in the last 15 minutes like an afterthought. A little break. A little memorization. A quick Uber. And then it was over.

The Austin trip was packaged as opportunity. Adventure. A reward.

But when I peeled back the layers, all I saw was a honey trap. Glossy surface, hollow interior. They gave us everything except the one thing that matters: freedom.

And me? I saw it for what it was. And I logged it. Filed it. Because the dream they sold me didn’t look like this.

My dream had more truth in it.

sections.title: Chapter Nine - The Training Manual
sections.html:
CHAPTER NINE

The Training Manual


WHERE THE CRACKS start showing and the mask begins to slide.

Back from Austin, the illusion was wearing thin. That whole trip had me feeling like I’d just walked off a movie set—props and performances everywhere, nothing behind the curtain. But it wasn’t until I cracked open the training manual that I really saw the skeleton of the machine.

I don’t even know what possessed me to start digging through it that night. Could’ve been the streak I was on—watching movies, decoding every metaphor, catching the strings behind the puppets. Or maybe it was just the feeling in my gut, that quiet hum that said, Something’s off.

But I remember the exact moment it began.

It was the sales records.

I was flipping through screenshots, looking at the “top dogs.” You know, the reps that made the leaderboards, the ones they put on the walls to keep everyone inspired—or controlled. 2022’s third place spot had 703 sales. But somehow, by 2024, two different guys had hit over 900. That wasn’t growth. That was a glitch. No one hit 700+ in company history until just two years ago—and now back-to-back 900s?

Something almost felt manufactured.

And that’s when the real question hit me:
Why don’t we ever do callbacks?

Why do we never revisit leads? Never follow up? Why are the rookies pushed out just to knock cold and leave cold? What if… we’re just warm-up acts?
Billboards with legs.

That thought twisted in my gut. What if we’re not supposed to succeed? What if they just send us to plant seeds, soften the neighborhoods, get faces out there—and then when we burn out, the managers sweep in to “close”? Callbacks would blow the cover. So they just… don’t.

That’s when I went back to the training manual. And this time, I read it.

First thing I saw: the schedule.

9:00 AM meeting. Bullshit.
We were out of the door by 8:15. Meeting started at 8:30 sharp.

Head to area at 10:00. Begin selling at 10:30.
We were already knocking by 10:30, usually earlier.

Lunch break at 3:00.
If you got picked up in time.

Hand touches first door at exactly 4:30 PM.
That word. Exactly. That’s when my radar lit up. I remember thinking—wait a second, this sounds like AI copy. Like they had ChatGPT write the damn thing. And honestly? It probably did.

I kept reading. The deeper I went, the weirder it got.

They had sections like “Sharpen the Axe,” “Push Through Soft Nos,” and a whole sermon on “The Mental Game.”
It started out sounding fine—maybe even helpful in spots. But then it turned.

There was one split I’ll never forget. It started as basic advice: Stay positive, keep your head right, mindset is key.
But then it hit this line—in bold:

sections.title: Chapter Ten - Sketchy From the Start
sections.html:
CHAPTER TEN

Sketchy From the Start


ALRIGHT, SO I don’t even remember every single thing they were doing—there was just too much. So let’s just start at the top. This was before we even went out into the field.

First thing I did? I Googled them. But immediately, I’m like—which one do I even pick? They had nearly two dozen separate Google pages for different “locations” across the country. I’m sure all of them might’ve been real. Most felt… manufactured. So I picked one randomly and started looking at the reviews.

And right away, the reviews were weird.

I mean, they all said the exact same thing. Just slight variations of: “Technician was excellent. Great experience. I’m happy.” That exact format. Over and over. And then there’s one that said, “The tech helped me over the phone and got my air conditioning working right away.” Huh? Air conditioning? Are we doing HVAC now? I thought this was pest control. But what really got me was that the company replied and said something like, “So glad we could help!”

I’m just sitting there like—okay, is that just an accidental review? Or is this just straight-up fabricated nonsense? Like… is this consumer fraud? Because it sure as hell doesn’t feel like pest control anymore.

But then came the cherry on top. A five-star review from my own manager. His name—right there—Cameron. Just right out in the open, reviewing the company he works for. I don’t even know what to say to that.

And it wasn’t just one location. Every single Astra Pest Control Google page I looked at had the same pattern: hundreds of five-star reviews with next to no negative ones. Like… statistically absurd. They were so skewed it stopped looking like a business and started looking like a coordinated PR campaign.

And it wasn’t just the reviews. When we were in Austin, we were staying at an Airbnb that, supposedly, Cameron had left a review for. Said the guy came out and did a great job. But here’s the thing—I was there. There was a mud dauber nest hanging above the door. I literally pointed it out and joked, “Hey, would you be interested in Astra Pest Control?” He laughed and said the guy had just come out. Like… what? There were also ants all over the yard.

So either the tech just came out and completely missed everything, or the review was fake. Take your pick. Neither answer is good.

But let’s keep going.

Then I started digging into the structure of our contract. We were classified as independent contractors—1099. But that didn’t line up at all. Because if you’re 1099, they legally can’t control your schedule, your location, your hours, or even your pitch. And yet… they controlled all of that. We had a set schedule. A detailed structure. Everything was dictated—where to be, when to be there, what to say. That’s a W-2 employee. Not 1099.

And then comes the pay structure.

When we made a sale, we only received 18% of the commission upfront. The remaining 82%? It was “withheld” and promised to us later, spread out slowly across a window from October to May of the following year. That’s eight months of waiting… for pay we already earned. And if that sounds shady to you, that’s because it is.

Now, before we ever even got out to the field, we had been told—verbally, never in writing—that we’d be getting $250 a week just for knocking. That was the expectation. That’s what they told us. No mention of a required quota, no terms and conditions, just: knock, and you’ll get $250 a week. Simple.

I believed them. I was fired up. I was running projections, working out how much I could sell, what my commission would look like. I had my framework. I was confident. Hell, I practiced on friends and family before we ever got to Texas. My cousin tried to resist—like, really tried—and I still closed him twice. I was ready.

But here’s what I didn’t see at first:

  • Fake reviews on every Google page.
  • A contract that misclassified us as 1099 while controlling our every move.
  • An 82% pay delay that made no legal sense.
  • A shady app that required customers’ credit card information directly.
  • A service contract that spanned 18 months… but with only 12 services scheduled.
  • Price anchoring scams—claiming that the “normal” price was $549, but because a truck just so happens to be in the area (even if it’s a brand new neighborhood), it’s “discounted” to $149.

All of it… layered on top of each other. And it hit me like a brick.

This wasn’t just disorganized. This was deliberate.

The veil had officially come off.

Meanwhile, back home, things were shifting. Zane and I were getting ready to move out. Cole was staying with us. His story’s important, too. He had gone down to Austin early—same time as Adam. But they wouldn’t let him sell.

Why?

Because he hadn’t memorized their exact script. That’s it.

Never mind the fact that he’d been studying my framework. Never mind the fact that he was actually ready to sell. They refused to let him go out. So he flew back. Stayed with us for a few weeks. That was kind of the final straw.

Because right before we were set to head back down, they told us we’d be stopping in Tennessee to take a licensing exam.

A licensing exam… for techs.

But here’s the thing—we weren’t techs.

We were sales reps.

So why were we being told to take a licensing exam for a job we didn’t do?

That… is Chapter 11.

sections.title: Chapter Eleven - The Exit Plan
sections.html:
CHAPTER ELEVEN

The Exit Plan


BY THIS POINT, I knew the whole thing was bullshit. Top to bottom. The company, the contract, the training, the “support.” It was all corporate sleight-of-hand wrapped in positivity platitudes and dollar signs. The veil was off, and it was time to go. But even knowing all that—leaving still hurt.

The day we moved out of the apartment was one of the heaviest I’ve ever had.

I had sold everything. My Xbox One. My VR headset. My Nintendo Switch. I sold my past just to buy a blank slate. Paid off the car insurance. Knocked out the bills. I was trying to do things right for once, you know? Just show up clean. No baggage. No clutter. Start fresh. That’s what I thought.

Zane? Not so prepared. He was still scrambling when I was already loading the car. Cole took his sweet time too, but I can’t blame him for that. We were all overloaded in our own ways. I wanted to leave by 4 or 5. I left at 8. Because of course I did.

The next destination? Murfreesboro, Tennessee. That's where the licensing exam was going to be—some official nonsense that none of us really understood yet. But we’ll get to that.

Zane and Cole rode together. Logan and I took my car. Two brothers in arms. He brought the nicotine, I brought the steering wheel. He traveled light. I packed more than I realized. My black Malibu was packed tight—everything I had left crammed into the trunk and back seat like it was the last escape pod off a sinking ship.

And then the skies opened up.

One of the worst rainstorms I’ve ever driven through. And I don’t say that lightly. We were on 75 South, and I’m talking full-on flashing tornado warnings. Cars were pulled off under overpasses. You know it’s bad when truckers are pulling over. But not me. No way.

I wasn’t stopping. I told myself I wouldn’t. Not because I had some death wish or something to prove. I just knew if I stopped, I’d lose momentum. And if I lost momentum, I’d lose everything.

So I kept going. Pushing forward, mile after mile, watching water blur the lines and lightning stitch the sky. And eventually, the storm stopped before I did. One of us had to quit first. And it wasn’t gonna be me.

We crossed into Kentucky. Then into Tennessee. Somewhere after 2 a.m., we rolled into Murfreesboro, exhausted but intact.

Astra had booked us a hotel. Nothing fancy—just off the highway. Logan and I got a two-bed room. It was simple, but after that drive, it felt like a king’s castle. We dropped our bags, flopped on the beds, and then…

Homework.

No, seriously. Homework.

After everything we’d just been through—six hours of driving, packing, storms, stress—they told us to complete a mandatory online training module. It was due by 8 a.m. It was already 2:30. I had just left my home. My life. Everything.

But okay. Sure. Let’s do some corporate homework before dawn.

We gritted through it. Crashed for a few short hours. And then… it was time.

The licensing exam.

The next morning would start the next story. But I’ll save that for Chapter 12.

This one? This was about leaving.

Leaving the comfort of home. Leaving the lies behind. Leaving the old framework of who I was and where I thought I was going. This was the clean break.

But even clean breaks leave scars.

sections.title: Chapter Twelve - The Licensing Exam
sections.html:
CHAPTER TWELVE

The Licensing Exam


OR: HOW I Failed a Test I Never Should've Taken and Still Almost Passed

We woke up bright and early, still half-drunk on exhaustion. We had to be at the testing center at 8 a.m. sharp where we pulled into what looked like a legit government building—one of those buildings where something official is supposed to happen, but no one inside really knows what or why.

And there they were.

The McLaren and the Mercedes, parked out front like royalty had arrived. The managers standing outside, arms crossed, like they were presiding over some kind of sacred rite of passage. But it felt more like a cult initiation. Just with less fire and more clipboards.

I was still trying to figure out why the hell we were even there.

We were salesmen, not techs. We closed deals at the door and walked away. No sprays, no traps, no chemicals. So why the licensing exam?

I didn’t get an answer. What I got was a room packed with forty other guys who all looked just as confused as I was.

And then in walked Darnell.

Darnell was the proctor. Legend. He had the calm demeanor of someone who’s been dealing with corporate bullshit long enough to see through most of it. He fired up his PowerPoint and started teaching—stuff we were supposed to already know.

Only problem? We didn’t.

There was no study material. No preparation. No outline. Nothing. We were just thrown into a real, state-level exam with absolutely zero notice.

He’s going through slides about invasive insects, restricted-use pesticides, state laws specific to Tennessee, and we’re all sitting there like, “Snakes are protected in Tennessee?” The only thing I was prepared to kill was a sale.

And even Darnell was catching on. Halfway through the presentation, he looked around the room, baffled.

“Did none of you get any of this ahead of time?”
“You guys get less and less prepared every year.”

He was pissed. But not at us. At them. Because he’d seen the pattern. He saw how these reps were showing up less informed each season, and someone on the other end was clearly dropping the ball.

So lunchtime hits. Me and Logan left to grab food. I had a little under $100 left of cash that my dad had given me before I left—my emergency fund. So I used some of it to buy us lunch at this knockoff Cane’s that apparently had one other location… in Kuwait. I still have no idea what that was about.

We come back, and the main room’s half-empty. Darnell still there, and I start chatting with him. Turns out the guy was full of wisdom. He told me about Tennessee regulations, how pest control really works, how the licensing works, how snakes are protected (still tripping over that), and what the exam was supposed to be for.

And it just confirmed everything I feared:
This exam was never meant for us.
It was for real technicians.

And we were just salesmen. Salesmen who had been told this was a requirement, who had been gaslit into thinking this was some critical step. No one told us what was on it. Our manager, Cameron? Completely useless. No one-on-ones. No prep. No communication. Just vibes.

Then, right before the test, someone finally dropped a Quizlet in a group chat. Over a hundred questions deep. I skimmed it for about 30 minutes, praying something stuck.

They handed us the test—100 questions. I finished in 15 minutes. Just raw instinct, pattern recognition, and caffeine. I handed it to Darnell.

“You done already?”
“Yep.”
Grades it.
“You got a 65. Needed a 70 to pass.”

Five points. I was five points from being a licensed technician in Tennessee. With no prep. No studying. No clue what I was doing.

If that doesn’t expose the entire system, I don’t know what does.

Slowly, more guys started trickling in. Grant (a different Grant—there were like seven of them) passed with a 72. Another guy got a 70 on the dot. One got a 69. And a good chunk didn’t pass at all.

Even Cameron. Year three. Barely did better than me. He’d been in the industry for years, and he still didn’t know enough to confidently pass a test on the work he supposedly managed. Either he was just as blindsided as us, or he didn’t care to learn in the first place. Neither answer was comforting.

And then came the final twist of the knife.

“You guys excited to knock tomorrow?”

Tomorrow.

We hadn’t even moved in yet. We didn’t have groceries. Some of us hadn’t slept more than four hours. I had just spent the last two days driving through storms, doing homework at 3 a.m., and failing a licensing exam for a job I wasn’t even hired to do.

But sure. Let’s start knocking.

So we got in the car and drove to Charlotte. The “Airbnb” we were promised turned out to be an extended stay with two twin beds shoved side-by-side, brown grime permanently baked into the tub, and a fridge that sounded like it was fighting for its life.

And that? That was home.

But that’s Day One. And that’s next.

sections.title: Chapter Thirteen - Day One in Charlotte
sections.html:
CHAPTER THIRTEEN

Day One in Charlotte


OR: THE CALM Before the Doorstorm

We didn’t even unpack that first night.

By the time we got to Charlotte, we had jumped forward a time zone and lost another hour of sleep. I think we rolled in close to 2 a.m.—maybe later. No time to settle. No decompression. Just collapse. We were told to be up bright and early. Classic.

I woke up the next morning in a fog. That week had already broken my sleep cycle into little jagged pieces. Four hours of sleep. Another four the night before that. And before that? I slept on a crappy couch at my family’s house just to be close to my dog one last time—he’s an old Great Dane, eleven years old. I didn’t know if I’d ever see him again. So I took the hit, for him. That’s the part no one sees when they talk about the “grind.”

Oh—and for context?

The plan, the one they told us back home, was that we’d be in Charlotte for about a month and a half. After that, we’d transfer to Nashville for the rest of the four-and-a-half-month season. That’s what they pitched. That’s what we signed up for.

That’ll matter later.

Anyway, morning hits. I don’t even remember my alarm going off. I get a call at 8:35 a.m. from Cameron. I just stared at it. Let it ring. Didn’t answer. It rang again. I let it ring again.

I physically couldn’t move. My body was done. Burnt. I fell back asleep.

Next thing I know, there’s a knock at the door—Zane and Cole. I drag myself out of bed. They’re like, “What happened?” And I’m like, “Man, I think I died for a few hours. I couldn’t move.”

I checked my phone. At 10:49 a.m., I texted Cameron:

“Hey, I don’t even remember this morning. I was comatose from the drive and the test. What do you want Logan and I doing?”

He responded:

“Just practice the pitch all day.”

What I read was:

Take the rest of the day off, bro.

So I did.

Turns out Zane and Cole didn’t even knock that day either. They got up early and went out with Cameron for a bit, but they didn’t actually hit doors. I think they were still trying to memorize the pitch. I was just relieved I could breathe.

So I took the day to move in. Finally.

At first, I was pretty upset about the setup. I thought I was going to have my own room, a decent space, some dignity. But no. This place was like… Nazi Germany in disguise. Corporate boot camp in an extended stay suite. I was this close to saying I felt like I was in Auschwitz—but let’s keep that one out of the final print. Bit heavy.

Instead of spiraling, I did what I always do: I flipped the energy.

I pimped that room out. Changed out the light bulbs for color ones. Rearranged the furniture. Put up lights. Pulled out every decoration I brought. I made that shitty little hotel room feel like home. Because if I was going to survive what was coming, I couldn’t let the space drain me.

Logan loved it too. He was happy. That made it worth it.

We even went and got groceries that afternoon. It was the first normal thing I’d done in a week. Just two dudes in a grocery store pretending this wasn’t all a little too surreal.

But of course, the illusion didn’t last long.

That night, Logan and I were told to head down to the managers’ room for a quick “meeting.” I think it was Jace’s room—Jace and Cameron were the two big dogs on the leash. The control freaks. They ran the Charlotte team like a dictatorship masked as a mentorship.

We waited thirty minutes to sign a contract. Not to be trained. Not to be mentored. Just to sign a document.

And this contract?

Unbelievable.

It said we agreed to show up every day on time.
That we would not return to the apartment during the day—at all.
That we would knock a hundred doors or make two sales each day.
That we had to take all criticism and feedback “with an open mind.”
That we weren’t allowed to complain—not to each other, not in texts, not in whispers.
We were only allowed to express negativity to the managers or the “vets.”
We had to participate in team activities.
Take ownership. No drugs. No alcohol.
And we had to commit to the entire full schedule, every single day, no exceptions.

Oh, and get this—at the top?

It was titled the “Knoxville Sales Rep Commitment.”
We were in Charlotte.

I hadn’t even technically agreed to follow it in this state.

But whatever. I signed it. Because I had to. Because we were already in the belly of the beast.

That was Tuesday.
I didn’t knock a single door.
I just braced myself for Wednesday.

Because Wednesday was coming—and everything I thought I knew about sales, about myself, and about what the hell I’d gotten into was about to be put to the test.

sections.title: Chapter Fourteen - Car Partners and Confessions
sections.html:
CHAPTER FOURTEEN

Car Partners and Confessions


WEDNESDAY BEGAN WITH a jolt. Not from caffeine, or the blare of an alarm, but from a message. A text, simple on the surface, yet existentially violating in its implications.

Car partners.

Two words that made my heart sink like a rock in tar. My first thought wasn’t who, it was why me? Was I really about to be forced to drive other people in my car after everything else they’d already pulled? Not because I didn’t like people—but because it was the principle. This was my car. My gas. My control. And now that was being stripped from me, too?

But then I looked again. Monday’s list said: me, Logan, and a dude named Grant. I was still driving, but at least it was with Logan, right? Alright, I thought. Not great, but not a full invasion. And then came the next day.

New list.

New names.

JJ. Grant. Eli.

And suddenly, it hit me—I wasn’t even driving anymore. I didn’t even get to bring my own car. I was just… assigned. To someone else’s vehicle. In someone else’s plan. It was like the last remaining thread of autonomy had been cut without my consent. What the hell even was this?

So I went outside, found Grant and Eli, and we loaded up. To be fair, they were cool. Chill, solid dudes. Grant was a bit of a chaotic driver—half-in, half-out of the real world—but cool. Just deep, deep into the Astra Kool-Aid. I knew from the start we couldn’t really be close. We were living in parallel realities. Same roads, different destinations.

He drove us maybe ten minutes down to this little office in a corporate complex, where we had our first official team meeting. And that was when the rest of the ridiculousness started to stack.

First: I didn’t have the Astra shirt on. I had gotten one. But it had a fat stain on it from a cruise a few weeks back. A white shirt, of course, so the stain never came out. That was all they gave us. One shirt. No backup. No replacement. Just: “Why aren’t you wearing Astra gear?” I think I had on gray shorts and a black shirt. Probably not the most professional, but I didn’t expect to be a corporate mannequin, either.

The meeting started. And honestly… I can’t tell you much about it.

Why?

Because I was mentally derailed by something much bigger.

A late-night call from the night before.

From her.

I’m not naming names in the book, but you know who I mean. Back home. Dayton. The girl who I thought was gone for good.

She called me—drunk. Like, blitzed. But it wasn’t just a drunk call. It was a confession. The kind of thing that pulls the rug out from under every coherent thought you’ve got.

She asked if I was home. I told her I was in Charlotte.

She asked about Zane.

And then she hit me with it: “I love you so much. I miss you. I can’t believe you’re not here.”

Boom.

The rest of the world melted away.

She was pissed I hadn’t gone to the bar to say goodbye before I left. She said it made her jealous to see me talking to other girls. She told me she wanted to marry me. That she wanted to spend the rest of her life with me.

Then—just when I thought my brain couldn’t take any more—she casually let me know she was taking a fat shit.

Most guys would’ve been thrown off. Me? I laughed my ass off. Because honestly, that’s rare. That kind of brutal honesty? Sexy. Weirdly sexy. It made her feel real. No masks. No performance. Just raw, unfiltered humanity—and somehow, that was the most attractive part of all.

But you have to understand, this wasn’t random.

This wasn’t out of nowhere.

There was this moment, months before, when she came over to my apartment, heartbroken over some guy. And I sat there with her, held her hand, told her she was beautiful, told her she deserved love and more. I saw the pain in her eyes, and I gave her something real. She cried. Then she sang. Hours of her just singing while I laid there listening. That night, something clicked in my head—but I never acknowledged it. Not until this call.

So while my manager was rambling about Astra policy or whatever, I was in another dimension, mentally back in Dayton, trying to process the emotional time bomb that had just exploded in my psyche.

That entire Wednesday morning was a haze. I couldn’t focus. Couldn’t think straight. Couldn’t believe what had just happened.

And just like that, the war between two worlds had begun: the one I was forced into—and the one I left behind.

That’s how Wednesday started.

sections.title: Chapter Fifteen - Curbsitting, Segways, and the Art of the Non-Sale
sections.html:
CHAPTER FIFTEEN

Curbsitting, Segways, and the Art of the Non-Sale


WEDNESDAY KICKED OFF with the illusion of momentum. I was warming up to Grant and Eli—both were solid guys. Grant had a kind of unhinged charm, funny and deep in the system. Eli, a bit uptight, but chill in his own right. We were assigned our territories, everyone dropped into some neighborhood like chess pieces on a board nobody really knew how to play.

They dropped me off on the side of a road. Literally. Like I was luggage. I asked if I could take a second to gather myself, and they were cool with it—but only as long as I didn’t curbsit.

Ah, yes. Curbsitting. Astra’s mortal sin.

Apparently, if you weren’t actively knocking a door—at all times—you were sinning against the cult. Sitting for any reason was taboo. You could only rest at lunch. That was it. Every second of stillness was seen as weakness. They had this idea that if your shoes weren’t on the pavement, you weren’t working. Never mind the fact that most sales came from actually connecting with people—not just knocking yourself into the dirt. But that didn’t matter here. Here, efficiency didn’t mean strategy. It meant obedience.

So, I did the only thing that made sense: I stretched. If they were going to make me knock doors all day, I wasn’t about to tear my damn quads.

Mid-stretch, I got a text from Grant—said he was swinging by to have me shadow him for a bit. Huge relief. Honestly, it felt like a gift. I didn't want to fly blind my first time out. I wanted to see how it worked.

He picked me up and we drove into this neighborhood that had a giant NO SOLICITING sign right at the front. We parked right next to it. Because of course we did.

Then it began.

Grant’s style was… something. High-pressure, rapid-fire rebuttals, a pitch for every protest. I watched him work Jared—a veteran having a party—with the kind of pushiness that made me feel like we were violating Geneva conventions. Jared had people over. He wasn’t interested. He already had a company. He had ant mounds, sure, but not enough to ruin his Saturday—or his life. But that didn’t stop Grant. He drilled into him for 20 straight minutes while this man just wanted to go back to the party he was hosting. It felt off. It felt wrong. It felt like coercion disguised as confidence.

To be fair, Grant was good. Like, technically good. He had cadence, rebuttals, posture, all that. But the vibe was off. He wasn’t connecting—he was cornering. And the worst part? That was the expectation.

Next house, same strategy. Knock. Pitch. Pressure. The tactic was to just keep people in conversation as long as possible, hoping they’d eventually cave from fatigue. We name-dropped Jared at the next door. We name-dropped Pamela after that. Everyone became a footnote in a manipulation sequence. It wasn’t sales—it was strategy without soul.

We talked a lot between doors. Grant and I vibed on some bigger-picture stuff—history, illusions, some real woke shit. He liked me. Thought I was autistic. Not sure if that was a compliment or an observation. Probably both. He could tell I was sharp, though. I was spotting holes in his pitch before I’d even knocked a door. Like with Jared—when he kept saying “it’s just not really a problem right now,” Grant missed the golden opportunity. So, I gave it to him later: “That’s your opening. It’s not a problem now, but it’s an investment for when it is. Once they’re in your walls, it’s a money pit.” Grant was impressed. Said he might use it next time. I think he knew I had it in me.

We talked to a hacker guy—white hat, I think it’s called—who drove a Mustang. Got him to sign some weird partial contract. Then there was the guy with the inch-and-a-half door crack, who wanted nothing to do with us. Grant wouldn’t let it go. Same lines recycled. Then came the guy with the dogs—who just wanted to go inside—and Grant kept using the dogs as leverage to keep the conversation going.

At that point, I realized: This was the culture. The pressure. The pestering. The over-the-line persistence. This was what Astra expected. And yeah, it made sense when I found out the company was run by Mormons. That snapped everything into place. The strictness. The conformity. The blind grind. The clean-cut smiles hiding a deeper control.

By the time we picked up Eli and headed to lunch, I was starving. I had pretty much no money left. I’d spent the last of it on groceries, making sure Logan and I had something to eat. I had about eight bucks to my name—and I wasn’t about to spend it on a sandwich. Not when I’d need gas soon. So I sat there at Jimmy John’s, stomach eating itself, watching these two scarf down subs while I silently realized:

I had everything I needed to start pulling the thread.

And that?

That’s where we’ll pick up next.

sections.title: Chapter Sixteen - 13 Hours to Nowhere
sections.html:
CHAPTER SIXTEEN

13 Hours to Nowhere


SO THERE I was. Sitting inside a Jimmy John's I couldn't afford to eat at, broke and starving. But clarity hit me like a cold sandwich to the face: I need a lawyer. No more waiting. No more hoping this thing would self-correct. I pulled out my phone, looked up employment law firms in the area, and landed on one—GJN (stand-in lawyer name ofc.)

I called. A guy picked up. Intake dude. No legal mind, just a receptionist with a script. “I’m so sorry to hear that… we’ll do our best to help…” You know, that kind of thing. The kind of thing that sounds supportive but lands hollow when you're partway through a longhaul scam dressed in khakis. I gave him everything. The whole story. He took it down. Said they’d be in touch.

I hung up thinking, okay, maybe I can breathe. Maybe there’s a way out.

So I got back in the car. Grant dropped me at a completely different neighborhood than where I’d started. Threw me off a little, but whatever. I was already floating in a haze of dehydration, low blood sugar, and a deep, growing distrust of everything around me. Still, I got out, looked at the first house, and took a deep breath. Let’s run it.

Door opens. Lady looks nice. Middle-aged. Calm energy. I choke. She says they already have a service, and I fold like a napkin. “Oh, that’s awesome! Have a great day!” Door shuts.

Next door—nothing.

Door after that—no soliciting sign.

And that’s when I realized: this neighborhood was dead. Dead energy. Dead prospects. Maybe one or two people answered. Most didn't want a single word. And why would they? In a place like this, when a stranger shows up at your door trying to sell you pest control, you’re not a salesman—you’re a threat. You’re the 15th guy this year pitching the same script with a different logo.

I kept pushing. Knock after knock. House after house. For hours.

And that brings us to the second big cult rule: the pitch script. Here’s how it worked. You start with “Hi, my name is [blank] with Astra. Here for the neighbors. You know how it gets out here right? Just out here helping with the bugs.” Then you say something vague about the neighbors, then you throw in the line: “If I can fit you in, I’m doing everything for over half off.”

And that’s where it all breaks down. Because if they give you any resistance—which they always do—you’re supposed to lean in. Not metaphorically. Physically. Literally. They wanted you to hold your iPad (or phone, in my case) out like a priest offering communion shoulder to shoulder and just go. Not to show them pricing. Not to show them value. No. To get their full name, number, and email address. Even if they said ‘no thanks’.

They wanted contact info above all else. That was the game. You didn’t need a sale—you needed stars. The app tracked them. The more stars you got, the more “success” you were seen to have. Not based on people buying—based on getting their data. Even when people didn’t want to give it.

I refused. I just couldn’t do it. I got a couple stars here and there, but nothing like what they wanted. Eli and Grant would yell at me later in the week. But I didn’t care. I wasn’t going to manipulate people at their front door just because Astra thought coercion was a skill set.

Still, I knocked. And knocked. And knocked.

The neighborhood was low-income. That’s not an insult—it’s just the truth. And it stood in direct contrast to the picture they painted back in training. Back then, it was all about the $400k homes, the dream neighborhoods, the place where you could close a dozen deals in an afternoon. These houses weren’t those. These were $180k homes with cracked driveways and barely-running Civics lining the streets. Every other person either already had a company or wouldn’t touch pest control with a 10-foot pole.

One guy liked me. Said I was a good dude. But his wife didn’t want chemicals anywhere near their house—even if they were supposedly “EPA approved and pet-friendly.” So that was that.

I had nothing to show for the entire afternoon. Not even a lead.

And then came the final punch: the email.

GJN emailed me back: Sorry, we can’t help you.

I stared at it. Felt my stomach drop. I called a few more law firms. P&P (other fancy typical lawyer). A couple others. No one wanted to take it on.

Nobody wanted to help.

I felt it settle in—this awful sense of isolation. The knocking wasn’t working. The pitch was hollow. The product wasn’t compelling unless you could manipulate someone into buying. And even the lawyers—people who get paid to take injustice and chew it up—wouldn’t touch this.

I was dehydrated. Broke. Alone.

By 8 p.m., it was pitch black out. Grant didn’t come pick me up until after 9. I’d been out since 8:15 a.m. I’d walked miles. Knocked probably a hundred doors. Nothing. No sales. No food. No legal help. Just a bunch of “what the hell are you doing here?” looks and a few patronizing pats on the back from strangers.

I got in the car and immediately got the managerial rundown. The “here’s what you did wrong today” lecture. I wasn’t rude. I wasn’t mad. But I tuned them out. Because I had already done the post-mortem a hundred times in my head. I knew what went wrong. I just didn’t have anything to fix it with.

We pulled into the lot near 9:30. I dragged myself up the stairs. Dead feet. Burned skin. And as I turned the corner toward my room, I saw the rest of the team waving me down.

Meeting time.

They had the nerve to make us sit there in a circle after a 13-hour day and talk about what we were “grateful for” and what we “could do better tomorrow.” I nodded. Smiled. Played along. I was grateful I hadn’t passed out. I could do better tomorrow by knocking 100 doors in a war zone.

By the time I finally got into the apartment, it was past 9:45. I didn’t even turn on the TV. I scarfed a half block of cheese, washed it down with chocolate milk, and stared at my phone until my brain shut off.

That was Wednesday.

Just Wednesday.

sections.title: Chapter Seventeen - Manifestation and Metal Chairs
sections.html:
CHAPTER SEVENTEEN

Manifestation and Metal Chairs


THURSDAY STARTED LIKE any other—too early. Another day, another battle against the storm of fake smiles and forced rituals. I was already drained, but I didn’t know yet how much more drained I’d be by the end of it.

The morning meetings had already started to morph into something out of a cult documentary. Picture this: rows of metal folding chairs—black, cold, and creaky—lined up like a budget seminar at a failing community college. In front of us, a big whiteboard framed by a scoreboard that tracked sales like it was a fucking game show. And in a way, it was.

There was a morning ritual. For each number of sales from the day before, there was a callout. A little chant. Zero? “Womp womp.” One? “He’s? On the board!” And so on, with each higher number earning its own cheer. It was cheesy. But I’ll be honest—it kinda stuck.

Transparency time: almost none of us youngins were doing well. Logan hadn’t closed a single deal. Zane wasn’t faring much better. Cole got a few—and funny enough, he had my sales framework on his phone. Coincidence? I think not. The guys who were selling consistently? They weren’t better talkers. They were just more shameless. They leaned harder, pushed further, crossed lines we didn’t.

Then came the prayer circle.

No, seriously. Every morning, they gave us “manifestation time.” But it wasn’t meditation or journaling—it was bow-your-head-and-pray-to-God time. Pray for sales. Pray to hit your number. Or, if not praying, text your friends and family about how grateful you were to be selling dead bugs for a living. Astra church was in full swing. Communion came in the form of iPads and price drops.

Then came the lessons. Real sales psychology twisted into something darker. They preached that “no” didn’t mean “no.” That there were soft no’s and hard no’s, and almost everything was a soft no. Which is fine in theory—sure, people hesitate. But the way they taught it? It felt off. Like if someone says “I can’t afford it,” you don’t take the hint—you push harder. If they say “not interested,” you lean in closer. They said it like gospel. Like truth. It was more than sales—it was indoctrination.

After the brainwashing session, we hit the streets. Grant dropped me off in another random neighborhood—this one a little rain-soaked but not unbearable. It wasn’t a hurricane or anything, just enough to make your socks damp and your motivation soggy.

I had a decent attitude going into it. I’d adjusted my pitch. I was a little looser, a little more natural. I wasn’t quitting yet. But the neighborhood? Brutal. It was plastered with “No Soliciting” signs like they were part of the HOA architecture. Nobody wanted to talk. I got a couple good pitches out, maybe. But no bites.

And while all this was happening, the girl—the girl—was still echoing through every mental corridor I had. That late-night call was chewing on me from the inside. Trying to hold that memory and a door pitch in my brain at the same time was like juggling a chainsaw and a snow globe. It wasn’t gonna work.

At one point, the sky just dumped. Full-on downpour. I was pitching this older Asian woman who was sweet as hell. She didn’t buy, but she did bring me water and an apple and told me to sit on her porch till the rain passed. That moment of kindness—it mattered. Probably more than she realized.

Eventually, I had to take a shit. Bad. So I booked it to a nearby grocery store, destroyed their bathroom, and blamed the half block of cheese and chocolate milk from the night before. Cheap calories, high density. Not exactly gentle on the digestive system, but it was survival food. That was all I had.

And that’s where I’ll stop for now. Because this day ain’t over. Not even close.

sections.title: Chapter Eighteen - Blackouts, Liquid Death, and The Prestige
sections.html:
CHAPTER EIGHTEEN

Blackouts, Liquid Death, and The Prestige


LUNCH WAS A lie.

Technically, we were scheduled to eat from 3 to 4:30, but that window was about as real as a door pitch “yes.” Grant knocked past 3—always did. So if you were lucky, lunch started around 3:25. And on Thursday, that meant Subway.

I still had no money. But the rest of the crew filtered in—Grant, Eli, Cameron, a few others from Astra’s dysfunctional fraternity of front-liners. I sat in the corner, solo. No complaints, no pity party. Just quiet, hungry acceptance. If “support your fellow man” was a real principle, it didn’t make it to the table.

I had water. Glass after glass of that crispy, crunchy, free-ass Subway water. I treated it like a feast.

After that, they dropped me back off in a different neighborhood again. I still had nothing but hunger in my gut and desperation in my chest. But I was locked in. Determined. I had to hit the quota. Just needed 100 doors. Something about the number felt like proof—proof I gave it everything, even if everything wasn’t enough.

So I knocked. Pushed. Hit street after street. No breaks if I could help it—God forbid the curb saw my ass. No sitting. No mercy. I was sweating, tired, barely functioning, but I kept knocking.

Then came the hill.

I’d just gone through 30 or so houses. Nothing. No answers. No sales. No interest. I got to the bottom of the slope, and something in me just collapsed. My body started giving out. Woozy. Vision went black. Like gone. I could barely feel my legs. My knees buckled, and I dropped my phone. Could barely even pick it back up after a couple minutes.

That was when I knew—if I didn’t lay down, I was going to pass out standing. So I laid on the sidewalk like some wandering traveler from an old novel, crumpled in the shade of a world that didn’t care.

I don’t know how long I was out. But then I heard it: “Hey! You good?” Didn’t answer. “Hey, man. You good?”

I came back to reality, sort of. I said yeah, I was fine, even though I wasn’t. He asked if I needed water. I said yes. He went inside the garage and brought me two ice cold cans of Liquid Death. Bless that man. Absolute angel. I crushed both like they were mana potions. It didn’t fix everything, but it gave me enough life to keep going.

I looked at the clock. About 7 p.m. I was close to the quota—85 or so. I needed 15 more. So I did it. Door after door. Hit over 100. I was crawling through the finish line, but I made it.

By 7:45, I was done. Fully cooked. Body fried. Mind toast. I took a detour to the grocery store again—round two with the bathroom—and got more water. Came back and found a nice little patch of grass. Laid down. Just tried to stay awake. Drifted somewhere between consciousness and survival.

Eventually, Grant pulled up. Past 9 again. Of course.

Same questions. “You make any sales?” Nope. “You gotta eat lunch to stay sharp, man. That’s stupid.” They hounded me. Mocked me. Cut me off mid-sentence. It was a lecture, not a conversation. The two of them in the front seat, me in the back. I was the rookie punching bag. Their rookie. Their failure to fix.

They didn’t ask if I could eat. Only why I didn’t. And when I mentioned I hadn’t eaten, just in passing, they pounced. Like that was the excuse. Like it was a decision. I wasn’t even complaining, just explaining.

Then they told me again—get stars. Get stars. Contracts. Pull up contracts. Coerce more people.

And then we got home. You’d think it would end there. But no.

The Waterboarding.

Two rookie reps had made a bet against two veterans. It was sales-based. Of course they lost. And as punishment, Astra-style, they were taken outside, behind the apartment complex. Someone grabbed a beach towel. Someone grabbed a 2-liter of 7UP. They wrapped the towel over their heads, and poured the soda down like some kind of off-brand hazing rite.

It wasn’t really funny. It wasn’t bonding. It was just fucking weird. The laughs were attempts to cope with the shock of our buddies drowning in sugary madness. Like some frat that lost its charter and forgot it wasn’t cool anymore.

Then some of the guys lit up—started smoking weed right there. One of the vets joined them. Another yelled at them. Even they weren’t on the same page. No rules. No standards. No consistency. Just chaos.

And that was the nightcap. The haze. The ritual. The spectacle.

I went inside, dead inside. Turned on The Prestige. And for two hours, I was somewhere else.

The Pledge. The Turn. The Prestige.

God, I loved that movie.

And that was Thursday. One more 13-hour odyssey through the absurd.

sections.title: Chapter Nineteen - Chocolate, Blackouts, and No Soliciting
sections.html:
CHAPTER NINETEEN

Chocolate, Blackouts, and No Soliciting


FRIDAY.

AT THIS point, it was less a work week and more a fever dream. A blur of sweat, rejection, corporate delusion, and melting chocolate. But we always started in the same place: the morning meeting.

Same folding chairs. Same prayer circle. Same scoreboard of shame. But this time, the vibe was off even for Astra.

One of the technicians looked like Negan from The Walking Dead. He was chill—one of the few with a smile still intact. And then, mid-chatter, mid-nothing, Jace—the guy running the meeting—just casually blurts out:

“Maybe I should kill JJ and hide his body in the wall.”

Everyone keeps talking. No reaction. Like that’s just a thing you say. I blinked. Did he just—? Yep. That happened.

Later, while we’re doing pitch practice, I’m standing there with Logan when Jace walks up, all smug. I look at him and go, “So, you’re gonna kill me, huh?”

He smiles. “Yeah, I was thinking about it.”

Naturally, I ask why.

“Cause you stopped knocking early.”

I told him—told Grant, too—that I literally blacked out. Like, body shut down. He shrugs it off: “Happens to all of us. Drink more water. Eat more food.”

Right. The food I couldn’t afford. The water I had to beg for at doors. Classic Astra solution.

Then Cameron, another manager, pulls me aside. Says he’s pissed because I went to the grocery store. I explain: I had to shit and get water. His response? I should’ve asked a stranger to blow up their bathroom. You know. Real normal behavior.

Anyway. Neighborhood time.

This one was promising. Nice homes, decent vibes. Felt like a place I might actually get one. I was a little dazed—between the girl stuff and the sleep deprivation—but I was locked in. Actually, that morning, I’d sent Dayton lady a message. Told her how I felt. She was already talking wedding plans. Florida, even.

Yeah. It was a weird morning.

I hit the pavement hard. Knocked 30–40 doors straight. Felt good. No sales, but strong energy. Until—

The Chocolate Incident.

See, I had this little pack of Hershey’s dark chocolate bars I’d grabbed at the grocery store. Thought it’d help with blood sugar. Tossed one in my pocket that morning. But I forgot one crucial detail: Nashville in the spring is a microwave.

I reached into my pocket, and it was chaos.

Wallet, charger, and a pocketful of gooey, unholy chocolate soup. The charger was brown like coffee. The wallet, somehow mostly unscathed. But my hands? Looked like I’d finger-painted with Nutella.

No point crying over melted candy. I cleaned up best I could and kept going.

Ran into two guys washing their car—renters. I pitched them. They were actually kind of interested, just didn’t like a specific part of the service. A few doors later, I realized the quarterly package would’ve been perfect for them. So I sat down on the sidewalk to figure out how to pitch it.

And that’s when Cameron showed up.

Of course.

He pulls up in the truck like a parole officer catching you at recess. I’d been knocking all morning, sat down for maybe five minutes, and boom—there he is.

He lights me up. Five, ten minutes of “You can’t sit, man. What are you doing?”

I asked for a water from his case in the back. Pretty sure that offended him more than the sitting.

Then he made me go back to the guys I’d pitched earlier. I didn’t want to go right away—I wanted to give them space. But he insisted. We went back, I emailed them a quote. Never heard back. Shocker.

Then came Cameron’s Pitch Parade.

He wanted me to shadow him. And it was… brutal.

First house? Woman doesn’t even open the door. He pitches through it. Like some reverse ghost. “Let me just keep you for a minute!” Door closed. Wooden door and elder knight standing firm.

Then he launches into this blackjack metaphor. “Good sales reps knock no soliciting signs. It’s like hitting on 16.”

No. It’s like asking for a slap in the face. A few doors later, we knock on one with a sign directly under the ring camera. The guy gets on and says:

“Hey, what does that sign say?”

Cameron stares at it. Defeated. “No soliciting.”

Yeah, buddy.

Then we see this house with fancy cars—a C8 Corvette in the driveway. Cameron gets excited. “Easy sale.”

We knock. Lady answers. Already has pest control. Cameron asks what they get. She lists everything we do, plus more, for less. Watching him admit she was set up? Priceless.

“I’ll be back,” he says. He doesn’t come back.

I hit a cul-de-sac before lunch. No answers. But one of the last doors? It was wild.

I was about to knock when the door swings open—scares the hell out of me. We both jump, laugh. Her daughter comes out. Turns out she’s the girlfriend of the guy renting the place. I pitched her, and she loved it. Total vibe. Got a star. But the guy wasn’t home, so I had to come back.

Still—one of the best pitches I’d given. I felt good. Hopeful.

And then it was lunch.
