sections.title: Chapter Twenty - Chick-fil-A, Chocolate, and Conscious Collapse
sections.html:
CHAPTER TWENTY

Chick-fil-A, Chocolate, and Conscious Collapse


SO IT’S FRIDAY afternoon, and Grant picks me up, right? The plan was Jersey Mike’s. That’s what we’d all agreed on, without me. I’m thinking, hey, cool—AC, outlets, maybe I can charge my phone, maybe not starve. But then Grant, in classic Grant fashion, swerves last minute and we go to this outdoor-only Chick-fil-A.

Let me say that again.

Outdoor. Only. Chick-fil-A.

Who knew that was a thing? Charlotte, apparently.

It’s 85 degrees. I’m sunburned to a crisp. My arms were about the color of a fire truck. The patio is packed with Astra guys—sporting their flashy watches, their sunglasses, their leased sports cars. But not a single one seemed to remember that whole “help your brothers out” speech.

Still no money, still no lunch. But plenty of water. Free water. Bless Chick-fil-A’s commitment to hydration.

I’m sitting off to the side, trying to scrape chocolate off my phone charger like I’m restoring a relic from the Old World. Not easy when every outlet is being monopolized by Segway guys. Because, of course, their fucking Segways need to charge more than I do. Makes sense. The vehicle comes before the person, right?

Eventually, I found a bathroom nearby—hallelujah. Relief. But by the time I came back out, Grant had been blowing me up. “Where are you?” “Ready to go.” “Let’s go.” I was two minutes late, but apparently that’s worthy of a federal offense in Astra law.

So we get back. Same neighborhood. And at this point, I’m pissed. I’ve had it. I’m thinking, they want me to knock? I’ll knock. I’ll knock so goddamn hard the HOA feels it.

I dumped all my gear—wallet, charger, everything—into a random service road off the neighborhood. Just tossed it into the brush like a survivalist. Chocolate-covered, heat-battered clutter I didn’t want dragging me down anymore.

Then I started knocking like a man possessed.

I had shorts on, some basic T-shirt, a hat with the sacred Astra logo. Didn’t matter. I was moving. I even got a call from my dad. Chatted with him for a bit mid-walk, which helped clear my head. But yeah—no sales.

And it wasn’t for lack of skill. I was getting good. Too good. Good enough to know, right off the bat, when someone wasn’t buying. Good enough to not waste my time. That’s the thing they don’t teach in sales. Sometimes it’s not about pushing harder—it’s about knowing when not to push.

I started realizing something else, too: the more honest I got with myself, the harder it became to lie for the sake of a sale. It’s like my soul kept whispering, stop selling what you don’t believe in.

But there were highlights.

The Black Neighborhood.

Now here’s the thing—every other rep complained. “Black people are so rude.” “They’re so racist.” Nah. Not true for me.

That day, the only kindness I got came from Black families. I had great convos, some laughs, some water, even got a guy to take my number down. Across the street, another dude gave me spring water in a slick glass bottle and got his number too. His dog was adorable. The white families that day? Cold. Dismissive. Usually hostile.

So I kept knocking. Hit the full loop. Knocked past sunset. I think I even went a few minutes past 8:30. Then I laid back down in the little wooded hideout where I left my gear. I was dead. Just needed silence.

But no.

Eli shows up.

Texted me. Asked where I was. Then rolls up like it’s pitch critique hour. I didn’t want to talk. I wanted to exist. But no, he wanted to workshop my pitch. So I gave it to him—about 20 seconds in, he’s chopping it apart.

Then he gives me his.

It was fine. The usual fake head nods, big smiles, overly polite tone. It was structured coercion with a smile. Again—not bad, just fake. Still, I could tell he meant well. He saw his rookie self in me and genuinely wanted to help. I respected that.

Grant finally showed. We rode back.

Another night. Another bullshit meeting.

“What are you grateful for?” “What can you do better tomorrow?” “Let’s all share our feelings and pretend this is therapy.”

I was just grateful to sit.

We finally went upstairs and crashed. That was it for Friday. My body was cooked, my phone was dying, my charger was frosted with cocoa, and I had nothing to show for another 13-hour day except a melted pocket and a deeper understanding of human behavior.

sections.title: Chapter Twenty-One - Saturday Sales Cult Sermon
sections.html:
CHAPTER TWENTY-ONE

Saturday Sales Cult Sermon


SATURDAY MORNING—THE sacred day. The Astra sabbath. The promised land of sales.

From the very beginning of the week, they were hyping it up like a damn religious festival. “This is the day the big dogs eat.” “You wanna make real money? Saturday’s your Super Bowl.” And, of course, there were rules.

Simple rules.

You had to knock from about 9:30 AM until 3 PM, minimum. But there was a catch—if you made two sales, you could leave early. If you didn’t? One of two options:

  • Knock until 4:30 PM, no break.
  • Or take a lunch and knock until 6 PM.

Which is just hilarious. Like, yeah, let me grab an hour and a half lunch just so I can earn another hour and a half of knocking. That makes total sense.

But they were proud of it. Proud of the hustle. They treated it like a badge of honor.

So here comes Saturday morning.

And they decided to give us a treat: breakfast at Panera.

You could almost hear the music swell. We were getting fed. Real food. Not gas station bananas or melted chocolate—Panera.

And then Jace ruined the fantasy in three words:
“You get what you get.”

They ordered a bundle of pre-selected sandwiches. About four types of some decent breakfast sandwiches. Just wait for the options to be called and hope for salvation.

I pulled a sausage croissant. And I hate breakfast sausage. Hate it. But I ate it. Because I was starving. Because I hadn’t eaten real food in days. It was still warm, and it was free, and I was grateful. Honestly? It might’ve been the best bad sandwich I’ve ever had.

They had coffee too. I poured in sugar, a squeeze of honey, a silent prayer that the caffeine would keep my soul tethered to my body.

Me and Logan—we were tight by this point. Sat together. Talked shit. Bonded over mutual suffering. Brothers in arms against the Beast. By the Beast, I mean Astra Pest Control.

Breakfast ended. Water chugged. Coffee down. Time to knock.

Dropped in a New Neighborhood.

It looked promising. Big houses, clean lawns. I walked a loop just to take it in—do a little vibe check. You can tell a lot about a place by the first few front doors. And it wasn’t bad. So I started knocking.

Nothing.

Nothing.

More nothing.

That 15% answer rate I mentioned? Yeah, still holding. If anything, it was lower. I was averaging one answer for every six or seven doors. And half of those were no's before I could even speak.

But something changed in me that day.

I stopped selling.

I started talking.

Not in some woo-woo “connect with people” way—no, I just... dropped the act. I was tired of pushing. Tired of pitching. So I talked like a person.

“Hey, sorry to bother you. I’m doing my best out here—this is a weird job, but it’s what I’ve got right now. Just wanted to see if there’s anything I could help with today.”

That kind of stuff.

I had some of the best conversations I’d had all week. People gave me water. They smiled. They actually listened for a second. Some of them even apologized for not needing anything. You’d be surprised how far honesty goes when the expectation is coercion.

But nobody wanted pest control.

And that wasn’t me being bad at sales.

Everyone already had it.

Seriously—like, everyone. Half the people I talked to had one of the big guys, or some better company. Hell, some had a guy outside their house spraying the yard while I was pitching. That’s how absurd it was. I felt like a vacuum salesman at a Dyson conference.

Meanwhile… the group chat.

Blowing up.

Contract after contract.
“89/79”
“99/89”
“129/99”

They were spamming numbers like a casino jackpot. But here’s the trick: none of it meant anything. Because even the “deals” were shit.

You’d pay, say, $89 up front and then $79 monthly. Which sounds decent until you remember that it’s recurring for 18 months, and if you do the math, that’s over $1,500 for some bug spray and a callback promise.

Ain’t nobody want to buy that unless you got a snake oil pitch and a manipulative smile.

But I still knocked. Hard.

Locked in. No curbsitting. No fucking around. Just house after house after house. Trying new stuff. Sharpening the blade. And not for them—for me. For the story. For the legacy.

By 4:30 PM, I was fried.

Body drained. Mind spinning. No food since morning. No sales. But I knew I had put in the work.

And that’s where I’ll leave it for now—standing at 4:30, drenched in sweat, holding my dignity and not a single signed contract.

sections.title: Chapter Twenty-Two - The $6.24 Bridge
sections.html:
CHAPTER TWENTY-TWO

The $6.24 Bridge


SATURDAY EVENING.

AFTER a full day of knocking, no sales, no lunch, and barely any energy left in the tank, 4:30 PM rolled around—freedom, in theory. Only problem?

No one was coming to get me.

The group chat lights up.
“Can someone get JJ?” – Grant.

Logan was already back at the apartment. He’d had to leave earlier—asthma meds. Possibly an inhaler. Either way, he’d been reprimanded for it. That’s how broken this place was: you couldn’t even treat a medical condition without catching heat.

Luckily, he saw the message. My keys were at the apartment. I had left them on the counter—intuition, luck, fate, doesn’t matter. Logan offered to take my own car and come get me.

And just before he arrived—Grant showed up.
Dropped off Eli and left again.

Eli sat with me. I wasn’t even on someone’s lawn—just on the edge, by a bush. Little patch of grass near the curb. But that wasn’t acceptable.

“Yo, we can’t sit here,” he said. “Can’t sit in people’s yards.”
Man, I wasn’t in their yard. I was on the edge of existence, just waiting to be picked up.

Then came Eli's speech. Again.
Because last night I had the nerve to talk to my dad during my route.
“You can talk to family before your shift. Or after. But not while you’re knocking.”

Then he got philosophical about neighborhoods. I’d told him earlier about one I’d seen—a super wealthy zone, right next to the one I was canvassing. I only knocked about twenty houses before I called it off.

Because they weren’t rude. They just didn’t care.
They weren’t buying pest control. They were buying time.
They already had contracts. Services. Systems.
To them, I wasn’t a salesman—I was a disruption.

I told Eli that. He laughed it off.
“No such thing as a good or bad neighborhood. All excuses.”
Every door’s the same. Every house is a number. Every no is just fear you didn’t push past.

I let him win. I had to.

So I gave him what he wanted:
“Yeah, I’ve been trying to tell myself that if I’m not making sales… it’s really on me.”

Boom. Hook. Line. Sinker.

His eyes lit up.
“Exactly! That’s the first step, man! You get it.”

Fake smile. Half nod. Please stop talking.

And right on cue, Logan pulled up—chariot of dust and redemption.
My car was filthy, covered in thick dust and sand from the Florida trip. The inside was a mess. But it was mine, and it was freedom.

We swung by a gas station. I had just a few dollars of credit left, across two maxed-out cards. I threw five bucks into the tank—just enough to get us back. I was hanging on by threads, but I had one thing keeping me going:

$250 was set to hit on Monday.

And that was my salvation.

Back at the apartment, I crashed for a bit. Let the weight fall off me. We had a dinner that night—a group dinner. Supposed to be this celebratory bonding thing for all the Astra guys.

Except some guys were still out knocking past 9 PM.

By the time we left, we found out we were going to some sleezy restaurant—the irony of that place not lost on me. She worked at the one back home. Not this one. But the echo was enough.

We walk in.

I had eight dollars (thanks dad).

I scoured the menu, looking for something I could order.
Kid’s meal. It was the only thing I could afford.

The big dogs sat at their own table. All the closers. The managers. The ring leaders.

Me, Zane, Logan, Cole, and the other rookies?
We were at the kids’ table—literally and figuratively.

They threw us a couple pity appetizers. That was... actually kind of decent. I’ll admit that. And I did eat. Chicken strips and a Sprite, probably.

Logan wasn’t going to eat—he didn’t have money. But before orders went in, Zane said:
“Cameron will get you.”

So Logan ordered a burger. Finally, a meal.

End of the dinner. Everyone’s full. Laughing. It’s time to pay.

Cameron comes by.

Zane. Cole. Cameron grabs their checks—he’d agreed to cover them.

Zane pipes up again:
“Hey, can you get Logan too? He doesn’t have any money.”

Cameron pauses. Looks Logan dead in the face.
“Did you make a sale this week?”

The whole table goes quiet.

Zane jumps in—“Come on, man. I’ll pay you back Monday.”

Cameron gives a little groan, a little sigh, a little eye roll.
“Fine.” Takes the check.

Then he looks down at mine.

$6.24.

That’s it.
Six dollars and twenty-four cents.

He looks at it.
Walks away.

Didn’t say a word.

This was the man who preached about helping your brothers, who rallied for unity and pushing past your limits, who talked about integrity, leadership, team. And over six dollars and twenty-four cents, he burned the bridge.

sections.title: Chapter Twenty-Three - Sunday's Quiet Storm
sections.html:
CHAPTER TWENTY-THREE

Sunday's Quiet Storm


SUNDAY.
IT WAS supposed to be the calm. The reset. The pause before another storm. But of course, even the pause was rigged.

We were told we had a “day off.”
What we really got was homework.

Two scripts:

  1. The Standard Pitch – the same lines we’d already been taught.
  2. The Switchover Script – for people who already had pest control.

It wasn’t actually new. It was just the same manipulative rhythm, packaged as a new weapon.
"Don't bash their company."
"Just match apples to apples."
"Out-coerce the competition."

Everyone already had their own version of it.
But memorizing it? That was Sunday’s gift.

This was our one “free” day after a six-day marathon of doors, rejection, dehydration, hunger, and humiliation. If I hadn’t skipped Tuesday’s shift, I wouldn’t have been able to get groceries at all. Stores were already closed by the time we were done every night.

I had a plan for that next check—Monday was payday.
$250 was going to drop, and that was going to change everything. Groceries. Energy. Maybe even a real meal. And yet, the whole time there was this quiet hum in the back of my skull:

What if the money doesn’t come?

I was brainstorming. I wanted to change the game. I wanted to take the wheel, even if the car was on fire. So I made a plan.

Offer people cash to make sales.

I didn’t care about the commission.
I didn’t care about the money.
I cared about breaking the spell—just once.
I wanted to sell something. Anything.
So I’d give people $50 just for referring someone—even if it meant I made nothing. I wanted to get some momentum. I wanted to feel human again.

That was Sunday.
That was supposed to be Sunday.

But then came the cookout.

They grilled hot dogs and burgers in the courtyard.
It smelled like middle school summer.
I didn’t want to go.

Felt like a trap.
I was convinced they’d lure us in with food and then spring some kind of psychotic meeting or pitch drill on us while we were chewing.

But then Logan called.

“No, seriously,” he said. “It’s just food. No trap.”

So I went. Grabbed a couple hot dogs—crispy skin, grilled right.
It was the first time in days I felt anything close to peace.

I even had a few bucks in cash, so I got a Dr. Pepper from the vending machine. Cold. Sweet. Spicy little cherry bite at the end. Perfect.

I sat.
I vibed.
I existed.

For just a moment—I was just a guy eating a hot dog in the shade.

But of course...

Knock. Knock. Knock.

Cole.
“Hey, you gotta come down. There’s a meeting.”

And just like that—back into the void.

Same living room.
Same tension.
Same manipulative cult energy.

This wasn’t a meeting. This was a funeral for morale.

Everyone sat in silence while Jace and Cameron complained about how wild the week was.
Training wasn’t finished. Numbers weren’t met. Expectations were shattered. It was all our fault. It was all our responsibility to lock in.

And then the real dagger:
“Everyone except two people made a sale.”

Cue the side eyes.
Me and Logan.

Not because we didn’t try.
Not because we weren’t capable.
But because we hadn’t given in.
We hadn’t swallowed the poison and smiled through it.

Zane and Cole?
They tried.
Hell, we all tried. But trying in this game didn’t matter.
Converting was all that did.

And then came the ask. I knew what was coming.
A massive rainstorm was on the way.

So I turned to Cameron and asked him, clearly and calmly:
“Can I go to the store tomorrow before we knock? Just to grab some rain gear?”

His answer?
“If you need something, ask someone at the door.”

I stared.
An umbrella?
A coat?
Anything?

“Just ask a little old lady at the door if she’s got one,” he said.
Jace backed him up.

These were the leaders.

I didn’t have a hoodie.
I didn’t have a poncho.
I didn’t have anything.

All I had was my phone, my last lifeline, which was now in danger of getting soaked and shorting out.

Logan’s iPad had already suffered water damage from light rain.
And now I was supposed to go out into a storm and just hope an old woman gave me an umbrella?

It was insanity.

So I went back upstairs.

I laid down.

I stared at the ceiling.

And I wondered what kind of hell tomorrow would bring.

sections.title: Chapter Twenty-Four - The Final Straw
sections.html:
CHAPTER TWENTY-FOUR

The Final Straw


MONDAY MORNING.
THE supposed payday.
But the only thing deposited into my account was silence.

No money.
No warning.
No explanation.

The $250 we were promised? Turns out, that’s only if you made a sale.
Not written down.
Not signed.
Just another verbal carrot dangled in front of desperate kids.

So I sat there, dead broke, no groceries, no food.
Nothing but rain on the forecast and rage in my chest.

Everyone knew.
Everyone.
They knew we didn’t get paid.
They knew we had no money.
They knew we’d been surviving on gas station protein bars and half-charged hope.

And they sent us out anyway.

Grant was gone, he had left for another city.
Logan and I rode with Cameron.
He played high-energy EDM like it was some kind of inspirational montage, while my world was actively collapsing.

But I had a plan.

North Carolina’s a one-party consent state, so I opened up Voice Memos on my phone, and I hit record.

And that day’s meeting?

Golden.

Same usual bullshit about pushing through no’s, power stances, fake smiles.
But then Jace—our almighty manager—drops a tactic straight out of a manipulation playbook:

“What I like to do is hand them the iPad... and walk away. Don’t say anything. That’s called... putting them on a leash.”

A leash.

That word didn’t even echo in my brain—it exploded.

He said it so casually, so proudly, like it was some legendary trick of the trade.
I had it recorded. Crystal clear. The Kool-Aid sermon in full clarity.

After that? We went to the gas station.
Cameron bought nothing. Said nothing. We just prepped to deploy into the flood.

Logan and I had a plan: split the streets. Stay close. Keep morale alive.

Cameron shut it down.

“No, you’re not doing that. JJ, you take the top. Logan, bottom.”

Cool.
No plan.
No warning.
Just divide and conquer I guess.

We got out of the truck.
We waited until Cameron left.
We looked at each other.
Neither of us had been paid.
Neither of us had anything.
But we had each other—for one last second.

And then...

The sky opened.

What started as a drizzle became a downpour, then became something biblical.
Sideways rain. Flood-style.
Rain that hits your bones and rewrites your soul.
Rain that says, “You don’t belong here.”

I knocked three doors.
Couldn’t use my phone. Screen too wet. Fingers too numb.
No way to dry it off, because everything was soaked.

So I found a tree.
And I started calling lawyers.

GJN, again.
They wouldn’t help.
Even with wage theft now in the mix, they called it the same case.
The new charges didn’t matter.
The system didn’t care.

I was invisible.

So I found a house with a “No Soliciting” sign and I knocked anyway—not to sell, but to survive.

“Hey, man, I’m not here for anything. I just need a place to sit for a bit. Can I sit on your porch?”

He let me.
Offered me water. Dry clothes. A dryer.

I said no. I couldn’t. I wouldn’t. I still had my pride, if nothing else.
But I’ll never forget that porch.
That man. That kindness.

Because they didn’t have to offer it—but they did.
The people I was trained to coerce were more human than the people who trained me.

I sat there, soaked and shaking, and realized:

This was it.

No phone.
No food.
No paycheck.
No umbrella.
No protection.
No future.

So I made the only call that made sense.
I called my sister.

“Can I borrow 20 bucks?”

She sent it.

And then I did the unthinkable.

I ordered an Uber.

I was done.

Done knocking.

Done bleeding for a company that never saw me.

Done being loyal to a system that laughed as I starved.

It wasn’t just quitting a job.
It was escaping a cult.

sections.title: Chapter Twenty-Five - Escape Velocity
sections.html:
CHAPTER TWENTY-FIVE

Escape Velocity


THE UBER PULLED up to the curb like it was fate on four wheels.
And for a moment—a brief, beautiful moment—I wasn’t alone.

I had Logan.

I wasn’t crazy. I was just right before everyone else caught on.
He called me back—“I’m on my way.”
Those words felt like a rescue rope thrown from the cliffside.

Thirty seconds later, he was there.
And so was the car.
Our chariot.

The driver? An angel in human skin.
Black woman, dreads, tattoos—real as hell and cool as hell.
Ex-trucker. Sharp as a blade. Heart wide open.

We told her everything.
She listened like she’d already lived it.
The cult. The rain. The fake pay. The lies.
The leash tactic. The 1099 disguise. The starvation games.
She got it all. She knew what they were doing.
And she wasn’t shocked—but she was furious on our behalf.

We made it back to the apartment—our forbidden temple—and no one even noticed.
No texts. No calls.
Not a whisper.
We were ghosts before we even walked out.

Logan packed fast.
Me? Not so much.

I’d built that place into a home—organized, optimized, mine.
And now I had to reverse-engineer the illusion.
Everything had to fit in my car.
Except the shoe rack. That one didn’t make it.
A minor casualty in the Great Escape.

I stuffed everything else in.
The memories. The frustration. The lessons.
Shoved it all into the trunk like the last page of a story.

And then came the fallout.

I texted Derek, Dean, and Miles.
Told them I was done. I’d left. I had escaped.

Derek? Immediately went for the throat.

“So you suck at sales, huh?”

Classic.

“You’re leaving ‘cause you couldn’t cut it. Zane’s staying ‘cause he can.”

Nothing about starvation.
Nothing about wage theft.
Nothing about the lies.
Just another smug diagnosis from someone who didn’t even read the chart.

And when I brought up God?
He hit me with the script.

“Only one person is truly connected to God. no humans can be Gods idiot.”

So I asked the question:

“What the fuck was Jesus if not human?”

And just like that, the conversation short-circuited.
He deflected.
Changed the subject.
Truth does that.

But I didn’t need validation.
I already had my proof.
Because I was free.

We pulled into a gas station.
A pit stop between the warzone and the afterlife.
I bought a drink with what little was left.
Logan sat beside me, silent but present.

And then...

The phone buzzed.

A text.
The Text.

The one I’d been waiting for.

It wasn’t just from a contact.
It was from Cameron

It was confirmation. It was validation. It was the moment.

sections.title: Chapter Twenty-Six - The Exit Wound
sections.html:
CHAPTER TWENTY-SIX

The Exit Wound


YOU DON’T ALWAYS leave with a bang.
Sometimes you leave with a receipt.

A gas station. A borrowed twenty. A sleeping passenger.
That’s how it ended.

Until the text came in.

“So y’all quit or something?”

Straight from Cameron.

No hello. No concern. Just that.
Like we were tools that had wandered off the job site.

Logan gave the only answer that felt honest:

“Yeah, this shit ain’t for me.”

Cameron’s reply?

“Y’all wanna be techs? You can get hourly.”

Like he was offering us the floor scraps from a table we were never really invited to.
Six days of hunger, rain, wage theft, and mental warfare... and the reward was an offer to chase cockroaches for scraps.

Logan politely declined.
I said I was done, too.

And that’s when the spin began.

“Wait, so you're quitting?”

No, Cameron. I never said that.
Not until you did.

So I asked the question:

“Just checking—are Logan and I not getting paid?”

And the mask fully came off.

“Base pay only applies if you make a sale. You didn’t.”

No warning. No courtesy. No food.
Just confirmation: we were expected to survive on nothing.

He claimed to be shocked I was quitting.
So I clarified:

“I didn’t quit. Just meant I’m done for the day. The rain was killer.”

And here’s where it got poetic.

“So why are you going home?”

I reminded him:

“Because I’m a 1099 contractor.”

And that’s when he brought out the contract.
The one they waved like a Bible until it didn’t suit them.

“You signed a contract saying you’d work a certain amount of days.”

So I dropped the real scripture. The legal one.
Constructive discharge.
Duress.
Retained rights.
Pay owed.

And his rebuttal?

“You didn’t complete any work. Commission only. You made no sales.”

That was it. That was all they thought we were.
No sales? No food. No surviving. No worth.

But the kicker?

“It’s all good. Enjoy whatever your future holds. I’m happy to be a reference.”

So I sealed the casket:

“So you agree I didn’t quit?”

And then came the line that burned it all down.

“You did. And it’s okay. You left before you completed your contract.”

Boom.

Not I quit.
Not I signed off.
Not I resigned.
I left.

And here’s the catch:
You can’t break a 1099 contract by leaving.
There’s no fixed location. No schedule.
You can’t breach a contract you’re not bound to follow like an employee.

So thank you, Cameron.
Thank you for putting in writing what no lawyer could have phrased more perfectly.

You left before you completed your contract.
Exactly. That’s all. And nothing more.

—

The rest?

Jack in the Box combos with better value than the entire sales program.
A car packed to the brim with escape.
A few bucks from family.
Logan asleep in the passenger seat.
Me, eyes locked forward on I-Whatever, rain spattered on the windshield, clarity ringing in my ears.

It wasn’t about pest control anymore.
It wasn’t about money.
It was about freedom.
About scraping together what love remained in the wreckage.

My dad paid for the food.
Told Logan he loved him.
Logan said it back.
It wasn’t weird. It wasn’t forced.
It was human.

That was the last scene of the chapter.

Not the text.

The ride home.

Until the text came in. “So y’all quit or something?” Straight from Cameron. No hello. No concern. Just that. Like we were tools that had wandered off the job site. Logan gave the only answer that felt honest: “Yeah, this shit ain’t for me.” Cameron’s reply? “Y’all wanna be techs? You can get hourly.” Like he was offering us the floor scraps from a table we were never really invited to. Six days of hunger, rain, wage theft, and mental warfare... and the reward was an offer to chase cockroaches for scraps. Logan politely declined. I said I was done, too. And that’s when the spin began. “Wait, so you're quitting?” No, Cameron. I never said that. Not until you did. So I asked the question: “Just checking—are Logan and I not getting paid?” And the mask fully came off. “Base pay only applies if you make a sale. You didn’t.” No warning. No courtesy. No food. Just confirmation: we were expected to survive on nothing. He claimed to be shocked I was quitting. So I clarified: “I didn’t quit. Just meant I’m done for the day. The rain was killer.” And here’s where it got poetic. “So why are you going home?” I reminded him: “Because I’m a 1099 contractor.” And that’s when he brought out the contract. The one they waved like a Bible until it didn’t suit them. “You signed a contract saying you’d work a certain amount of days.” So I dropped the real scripture. The legal one. Constructive discharge. Duress. Retained rights. Pay owed. And his rebuttal? “You didn’t complete any work. Commission only. You made no sales.” That was it. That was all they thought we were. No sales? No food. No surviving. No worth. But the kicker? “It’s all good. Enjoy whatever your future holds. I’m happy to be a reference.” So I sealed the casket: “So you agree I didn’t quit?” And then came the line that burned it all down. “You did. And it’s okay. You left before you completed your contract.” Boom. Not I quit. Not I signed off. Not I resigned. I left. And here’s the catch: You can’t break a 1099 contract by leaving. There’s no fixed location. No schedule. You can’t breach a contract you’re not bound to follow like an employee. So thank you, Cameron. Thank you for putting in writing what no lawyer could have phrased more perfectly. You left before you completed your contract. Exactly. That’s all. And nothing more. — The rest? Jack in the Box combos with better value than the entire sales program. sections.title: Chapter Twenty-Seven - The Last Door
sections.html:
CHAPTER TWENTY-SEVEN

The Last Door


IT’S FUNNY HOW you always think the ending is going to be the dramatic part.

Sometimes it’s just the truth that hits the hardest.

You expect rage. You expect final explosions.
But instead, it’s a login screen that won’t let you in.

Invalid.

That was the word.

Not “terminated.”
Not “offboarded.”
Not even a goodbye.

Just invalid.

After weeks of rain, hunger, wage theft, cult tactics, psychological warfare, and a long-ass drive home…

They quietly deleted my app access.

I was actually still trying to make sales from home.

Not a contract termination.
Not a dispute resolution.
A passive-aggressive backend flick of a button.

I wasn’t worth a sentence. Just a database update.

And in doing that?

They made a case stronger than I ever could have alone.

They turned a little suspicion into proof.
They crossed the line I hoped they were too smart to cross.

So, I came home.
The room wasn’t ready—but I made it ready.
I turned the ruins into headquarters.
And when the walls finally stopped closing in, I did what only I could:

I wrote it all down.

Not to be a whistleblower.
Not to start a war.
But because the truth was too heavy to carry alone.

Logan came home.
Zane came home.
Cole came home.

And still—no real closure, no accountability.
Just a parade of contradictions and a corporate silence that roared louder than anything they’d said during their morning meetings.

And the biggest twist?

It wasn’t a story about sales.

It never was.

It was a story about power, and what happens when you strip everything away from a person and expect them to sell their soul for scraps—and they don’t.

sections.title: Afterword
sections.html:
AFTERWORD


BY THE TIME you finish a book like this, you’re left wondering—was it all worth it?


The answer depends on who you are.


If you were there, if you felt the cold metal of iPhone in your hand, if you gave the same pitch a hundred times a day, if you crushed the board or crumbled in the van—then you already know.


This wasn’t just a job. It was a pressure cooker. A cult. A catalyst. A classroom.


A lot of people will read this and see it as a warning. But if you’re like me you’ll see it as a tribute. Because no matter how insane it got, we were there. We lost our minds. And we came back with the story.


That’s what The High Road really is: a story. One that wasn’t supposed to be told—but needed to be.


So if you made it this far, thank you. You walked the line with me. Maybe now you see the game a little clearer. Maybe now, you know what not to sell.


Any maybe—just maybe—you’re finally ready to sell yourself on something bigger.


Take the high road. Every time.

-JJ

See you on the next high road.

sections.title: About the Author
sections.html:
ABOUT THE AUTHOR


JAMES JOHNSON IS a Midwestern original with a knack for turning chaos into clarity and door-knocking into philosophy. From pushing sales in the sweltering heat to rewriting the rules of the game, he’s seen the grind from the inside—and lived to write about it.


A storyteller at heart and a strategist by nature, James captures real-life transformation with raw honestly, humor, and a refusal to flinch. Whether you’ve knocked doors yourself or just wondered what it’s like behind the scenes of a high octane sales cult, this book gives you the front-row seat you didn’t know you needed.


He writes from experience. He writes from memory. But most importantly, he writes from the high road.
